label: Person
name: Caravaggio
summary:
Michelangelo Merisi da Caravaggio (1571–1610) was an Italian painter whose revolutionary use of chiaroscuro—dramatic contrasts of light and shadow—transformed European art. Working in Rome, Naples, Malta, and Sicily, he painted directly from life onto canvas without preliminary drawings, a radical departure from Renaissance studio practice.

Caravaggio's masterworks include 'The Calling of Saint Matthew' (1599–1600), 'Judith Beheading Holofernes' (c. 1598), and 'The Entombment of Christ' (1603–1604). His unflinching realism depicted saints as ordinary people with dirty feet and weathered faces, shocking patrons accustomed to idealized religious imagery.

His violent temperament led to a murder conviction in Rome in 1606, forcing him into exile. He spent his final years fleeing justice while producing some of his most powerful works. He died at age 38 under mysterious circumstances on a beach at Porto Ercole.

Caravaggio's influence spawned an entire movement—Caravaggism—that spread across Europe through followers like Artemisia Gentileschi, Georges de La Tour, and Jusepe de Ribera. 'What he did was to make the painting itself the event,' as critic Robert Hughes noted.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Caravaggio's innovative use of chiaroscuro influenced generations of artists, including Rembrandt and Vermeer, and paved the way for Baroque art. His unflinching realism also challenged traditional depictions of saints in Christian art.
